name: Mars Life Explorer
short_status: Still a concept as of 24 August 2026, with no new start, funding line or launch date. The 2022 decadal survey made this ice-drilling lander NASA's top medium-class Mars mission, to follow sample return's peak spending.
tagline: NASA · United States · Lander · 2021 · Announced Planned
stats: depth its drill would reach into mid-latitude ground ice
launch date assumed in the decadal survey's own independent cost and technical evaluation

facts.label: What it is for
facts.value: In the decadal survey's words, the focus of Mars Life Explorer is to seek extant life and assess modern habitability. That is a different target from Perseverance and sample return, which look at the ancient rock record. In the survey's words the notional mission concept examines Mars's lowest-latitude ice deposits, which preserve a record of recent climate change and may provide a recent habitat. Nothing has been built.

facts.label: Its formal priority
facts.value: The 2023-2032 decadal survey, Origins, Worlds, and Life, considered four medium-class Mars missions and put two through independent evaluation. It states that the committee ranked MLE as the highest priority medium-class mission for the MEP, and recommends that subsequent to the peak-spending phase of MSR, the next priority medium-class mission for MEP should be Mars Life Explorer. The conditional clause matters: MLE was recommended to follow sample return, never to replace it.

facts.label: Where the design comes from
facts.value: A mission concept study report written by JPL in 2021 for the decadal survey, cited by the survey as NASA 2021h and hosted alongside the other decadal concept studies in a shared drive folder. The decadal's own summary of it is the most accessible public description of the design.

facts.label: What it would measure
facts.value: Four objectives as studied: search for organic molecules, non-equilibrium gases and isotopes associated with ice and regolith and evaluate their possible biological origin; assess the habitability of the near-subsurface for required elements, microbial energy sources and compounds toxic to microbes; quantify the down-borehole thermophysical properties of the ice and ice-cemented regolith and any role for liquid water; and determine what preserves, modifies or destroys these ice deposits in the modern climate.

facts.label: The payload as studied
facts.value: A biosignature detection suite built around DRaMS with evolved gas analysis and a miniature tunable laser spectrometer; a chemistry, mineralogy and conductivity suite combining CheMinX, MECA and evolved gas analysis; a wind, water and radiative flux suite with an anemometer, a tunable laser spectrometer and MEDA-derived temperature, pressure and thermal infrared sensors; a downhole sensor and imager; and a context camera.

facts.label: The vehicle as studied
facts.value: A lander that stays where it touches down. A single-segment 2 metre drill on a three-degree-of-freedom boom with its own avionics box, a biobarrier, a gas sample transfer system, two 5.8 square metre Ultraflex solar arrays, an 80 amp-hour lithium-ion battery, hydrazine propulsion, redundant avionics, UHF and X-band radio, a 3.65 metre aeroshell and a cruise stage with a 5 square metre fixed array. The study assumed launch on a recoverable Falcon Heavy.

facts.label: How long it would work
facts.value: A 34-month mission life: 10 months of cruise, 3 months of sampling and analysis, then 21 months of meteorology only. The long tail is deliberate. Watching one full Martian year is what tells you whether the ice deposit is currently stable or currently vanishing.

facts.label: Where it would land
facts.value: The decadal's technical evaluation gives the destination as the Martian surface at 40 to 50 degrees north latitude. The Planetary Society, reporting in August 2022 on the concept, named Arcadia Planitia as one proposed landing zone. Site choice is a genuine engineering tension: ice sits closer to the surface further north, and further north costs power and heat.

facts.label: Cost, contested
facts.value: The Planetary Society reported in August 2022 that MLE is slated to cost 1.1 billion dollars. The decadal survey's own independent cost figure for MLE is presented in a graphic in Appendix C and is not in the readable text of the report, so we cannot quote it. The decadal notes generally that its independent estimates run higher than the numbers mission advocates supply, so 1.1 billion should be read as a study-team figure rather than an independent one.

facts.label: Launch and arrival dates, contested
facts.value: Two dates circulate for the same concept and they do not measure the same thing. The Planetary Society reported in 2022 that MLE was "a fixed landing platform launching in the early-to-late 2030s" and "could land on Mars in 2033"; in that piece 2033 is when MLE would arrive. It is not the year it would launch. The decadal survey's independent technical and cost evaluation separately assumed a nominal launch of May 2035. Neither is a schedule. There is no project to schedule.

facts.label: Technical risk rating
facts.value: The decadal's evaluation rated MLE medium-low: moderate new development, adequate margins and moderate risk to major objectives. Its named challenges were landing accurately enough to reach accessible ice with a drill that cannot drive anywhere, lander mass growth beyond the entry and descent system's limits, design churn from payload uncertainty, and power sizing driven by that same uncertainty.

facts.label: The rival that already exists on paper
facts.value: Icebreaker, the NASA Ames ice-drilling lander proposed to Discovery in 2015 and 2019, would drill to the same 2 metres in the same mid-latitude ice. Its team states that Icebreaker could address most of the science goals of the decadal-prioritised MLE concept. The two are separate proposals with overlapping targets, and only one of them has ever been through a competitive review.

facts.label: The precondition has not happened
facts.value: MLE was recommended to follow the peak spending phase of Mars sample return. Congress declined to fund sample return in the fiscal 2026 appropriations bill. At the LPSC town hall on 16 March 2026, NASA planetary science division director Louise Prockter said of MSR that at this time we are standing by for future budget guidance and direction from the agency as to how we might proceed.

facts.label: The money in 2026
facts.value: NASA's planetary science division received 2.54 billion dollars for fiscal 2026, above the 1.89 billion the administration requested but below the 2.72 billion it received in each of fiscal 2024 and 2025. Prockter told the community that the division could not continue everything and that hard strategic choices were coming. She also said the next New Frontiers call is expected in 2027 and Discovery will not solicit before 2028.

facts.label: What the Mars community said in 2026
facts.value: In a memo circulated on 17 June 2026, MEPAG leadership wrote that the Mars Exploration Program had been directed to absorb the Skyfall payload on the Space Reactor-1 demonstration mission within its own budget, largely under the Mars Future Missions line, effectively eliminating any new developments or missions until after that launch, and that the line holds about 110 million dollars. In statements released for community review on 1 July 2026 MEPAG wrote that the current set of planned Mars activities does not reflect the Mars Future Plan or Decadal Survey priorities, and that the United States faces a ten-year gap in competed science mission and payload opportunities at Mars.

facts.label: What NASA is flying to Mars instead
facts.value: On 24 March 2026, in a set of announcements called Ignition, NASA said it would build out a Mars telecom network and start a new mission, Space Reactor-1 Freedom, aiming to launch before the end of 2028 using nuclear electric propulsion and to deploy a payload of Ingenuity-class helicopters to scout landing sites and search for subsurface water ice. So the vehicles currently headed for Martian ice are those helicopters, and MLE is not among them.

timeline: JPL completes the Mars Life Explorer mission concept study report for the 2023-2032 decadal survey, one of a set of concept studies commissioned to give the survey something concrete to evaluate.

The decadal survey Origins, Worlds, and Life is released. It ranks MLE the highest-priority medium-class mission for the Mars Exploration Program and recommends it as the next such mission after the peak spending phase of sample return.

The Planetary Society publishes the first detailed public account of the concept, reporting a cost of 1.1 billion dollars, a launch in the early-to-late 2030s and a possible arrival at Mars as early as 2033, and quoting Amy Williams and Bethany Ehlmann on why modern habitability is now a tractable target.

With sample return in trouble, the Mars community and NASA publish a plan for a sustainable science programme at Mars covering the next twenty years, the document later referred to as the Mars Future Plan.

TRIDENT, the Honeybee Robotics rotary-percussive drill baselined by the competing Icebreaker concept, reaches the Moon. The lunar unit NASA describes is 1 metre long; the Mars version Icebreaker baselines is 2 metre capable on Intuitive Machines' IM-2. The lander tips over and the mission lasts about ten hours, but the drill runs.

A white paper prepared for the MEPAG Search for Life Science Analysis Group workshop argues that MLE's own science traceability matrix emphasises habitability and organic chemistry over direct life detection, and proposes instrument upgrades for agnostic life detection before crewed missions contaminate the ground.

The fiscal 2026 appropriations bill covering NASA finally passes. Planetary science gets 2.54 billion dollars, far above the administration's 1.89 billion request but below the 2.72 billion of the two previous years. Mars sample return, MLE's stated precondition, is not funded.

At the LPSC planetary science town hall, division director Louise Prockter says not everything can continue, that a fiscal 2026 operating plan will name what changes, and that the next Discovery call will not come before 2028.

NASA's Ignition announcements set the near-term Mars agenda: a Mars telecom network, and Space Reactor-1 Freedom, a nuclear electric propulsion mission aiming to launch before the end of 2028 carrying Ingenuity-class helicopters to look for subsurface ice.

A MEPAG memo tells the Mars community that the Mars Exploration Program has been directed to absorb Skyfall within its own budget, largely under a Mars Future Missions line holding about 110 million dollars, effectively eliminating new mission starts until after that launch.

MEPAG releases findings and statements of concern for community review, saying the planned Mars activities do not reflect the Mars Future Plan or decadal priorities and that the United States faces a ten-year gap in competed science mission and payload opportunities at Mars.

images.caption: An artist's concept of the Mars Life Explorer standing on rocky ground under a pale orange sky: a lander in the Phoenix and InSight mould, with two circular fan-fold solar arrays spread either side, instrument boxes on the deck, and a tall vertical drill mast reaching down to the surface beside the leg. The Planetary Society captions it as the Mars Life Explorer operating on the surface with its drill deployed. Nothing has been built.

A HiRISE excerpt from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showing a small fresh impact crater in the northern mid-latitudes, a bright white patch of excavated ice at its centre surrounded by a dark blast scar on rippled orange ground, with a 100 metre scale bar. NASA's record states that the impact exposed bright ice that had been hidden just beneath the surface at this location.

The Subsurface Water Ice Mapping map, a grey shaded-relief Mars base with the Tharsis volcanoes and Valles Marineris across the lower half and a broad blue wash covering the northern plains, marking where NASA missions have detected subsurface water ice. Triangles are past and present landed missions, circles are ice-exposing impact craters. NASA's record states that the project mapped from the equator to 60 degrees north, hunting ice in the mid-latitudes: far enough toward the pole for water ice to be plentiful, but close enough to the equator to avoid the coldest temperatures on Mars.
